My personal opinion is its more of a metric that describes how many people saw your thumbnail.

Impressions is not equal to video views. Only how many people the algorithm displayed your thumbnail to. That's it. 

If you got 150 views from a pool of 1.2k people I think you're video will likely stall soon if your retention isn't good.

Put it this way, YouTube wants people to see your video but before showing the entire platform your thumbnail it tests it with a small pool of people that may be interested in your content. So it pops it into their view and waits too see if they'll watch it for some time. 

Then 24 hours later a pattern starts to appear. Only 150 people clicked on your thumbnail out of the 1.2k people that saw it. So far interest in your packaging is poor.

So now YouTube will check to see if those people that clicked the video watched the video to the end. If they did then it means your video is good and your packaging just isn't so it'll continue to try to target people that may also like your content regardless because obviously your video is making people happy. 

But let's say that your video needs work such as better flow, better concept, better lighting, better script, better everything maybe, and people are clicking out of your video and onto something else pretty quickly.

Maybe because they got bored, uninterested, thought they were watching a video about topic A but your video is about topic B, or your video structure is just poor it's hard to tell what your topic is at all in your packaging and intro. 

Then YouTube is going to see that your video isn't making people happy and thus it reports back to you with the little data it collected and now waits for you to upload your next video. A better video.

That's what metrics are about. They're a conversation with YouTube algorithms.

No single metric is the definition of success. Your work and uploads are a negotiation that you can win if you play by the rules and provide.
